page_hint: Ch 1 §1 KV cache as a concept (PDF ~p. 19)
quoted_clause: (vLLM blog, post dated 2026-04-22; retrieved 2026-11-15) [S6]
observed: The vLLM FP8-KV blog citation carries a retrieval date of 2026-11-15, but §7 'What We Still Don't Know' states the book's evidence position 'As of 2026-08.' A source retrieved after the stated evidence cutoff is either a stale-cutoff inconsistency or an unstated later cutoff.
evidence: §7 opens '*As of 2026-08:*'; the §1 citation says 'retrieved 2026-11-15.' If 2026-08 is the book-wide evidence cutoff (as the artifact-lock convention requires recording), a 2026-11-15 retrieval cannot be in scope; if the cutoff is later, §7's date is stale.
root_cause: Evidence-cutoff date not reconciled between the citation and the 'as of' statement.
correction: Reconcile the two dates: either update §7's 'as of' date to the true evidence cutoff, or confirm the vLLM retrieval date and state the book-wide cutoff once (Preface/evidence-boundary panel) and reference it. Ensure no citation post-dates the declared cutoff.

quoted_clause: ~10 requests/s average
observed: The averaging window for '~10 requests/s average' is unspecified. At 24/7 this implies ~25.9M req/month; at 22 business days x 8 h it implies ~6.3M req/month. The book's canonical ledger elsewhere carries '6.24M req/mo,' which is only consistent with the business-hours reading. The chapter does not state which window applies, so a reader reconciling the two figures cannot tell whether they agree.
evidence: 10 req/s x 2,592,000 s/mo = 25.92M req/mo (24/7); 10 req/s x 633,600 s/mo (22 d x 8 h) = 6.336M req/mo ~ 6.24M. The chapter gives no window, so both readings are open and only one matches the canonical monthly figure.
root_cause: Denominator/operating-point not specified for a rate that is later converted to a monthly volume.
correction: State the averaging window explicitly at first use (e.g., '~10 req/s averaged over business hours' or 'over 24/7'), and make it consistent with the canonical monthly request figure in Ch 4. If the canonical figure is business-hours-based, say so here.
acceptance_test: The chapter states the averaging window, and 10 req/s x window reproduces the canonical monthly request count used downstream.

quoted_clause: The "128 to a few thousand" range applies to *retrieval* embeddings
observed: The lower bound of 128 for retrieval-embedding width is unusually small; common dedicated retrieval encoders are 384–1536, and 128 is rare. The range is not sourced and may mislead a reader into thinking 128-dim retrieval embeddings are common.
evidence: Typical retrieval embedding widths: 384 (MiniLM-class), 768 (BERT-class), 1024/1536 (commercial APIs), 3072/4096 (large). 128 is atypical; the chapter gives no example at that width.
root_cause: Unsourced range with an atypical lower bound presented as the retrieval-embedding range.
correction: Either raise the lower bound to the commonly observed minimum (e.g., 'a few hundred to a few thousand') or cite an example model at 128 if one is intended. If the range is meant to be exhaustive, source it.
acceptance_test: The stated range is either sourced or its bounds are defensible from named examples.

chapter: Chapter 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference
quoted_clause: It becomes bandwidth-saturating above ~5 concurrent sequences per GPU (~40 per host) and compute-bound above ~295 concurrent sequences per GPU.
observed: The two thresholds are derived from incompatible batching models. The ~5-sequence threshold follows only if each sequence independently streams the full weight shard (no weight-read amortization): 5 × 17.5 GB / 25 ms ≈ 3.5 TB/s. The ~295 threshold follows from the roofline ridge with amortized weight reads: AI ≈ B FLOP/byte and ridge ≈ 295 FLOP/byte. Under amortized continuous batching, HBM utilization at 25 ms TPOT is ~17.5 GB / (25 ms × 3.35 TB/s) ≈ 21% and does not rise with batch size; under no amortization, the compute-bound threshold would be ~1,400 sequences, not ~295.
evidence: Recomputation from the chapter's own numbers: per-GPU shard 17.5 GB, HBM 3.35 TB/s, TPOT 25 ms, H100 BF16 dense 989 TFLOPS, ridge 989/3.35 ≈ 295. The text itself says continuous batching amortizes weight reads, so the ~5 threshold cannot coexist with the amortized model used for ~295.
root_cause: Mixing a per-sequence weight-streaming model with an amortized-batch roofline model in one sentence.
correction: State the batching assumption explicitly. Under amortized weight reads, HBM utilization is independent of batch size at fixed TPOT; the step becomes bandwidth-limited only when TPOT approaches the weight-read time (~5.2 ms), not at ~5 sequences. Under no amortization, bandwidth saturates near B≈5 but compute binds near B≈1,400. The ~295 figure is the roofline ridge, not an SLO occupancy threshold.
acceptance_test: Recompute both thresholds from the stated batching model; verify that the same model produces both numbers and that the text no longer implies HBM saturation at ~5 sequences while also claiming weight-read amortization.

chapter: Chapter 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference
quoted_clause: ~2,000 registered employees, each roughly as active as the canonical scenario (~10 requests/s average, peaks ~40 rps)
observed: If each of 2,000 employees were as active as the canonical scenario at 10 rps average, aggregate traffic would be ~20,000 rps, not 10 rps. The next paragraph uses 10 rps average and 40 rps peak as the aggregate, contradicting the 'each' phrasing.
evidence: 2,000 × 10 rps = 20,000 rps. The downstream token rates (92,000 input tokens/s, 3,000 output tokens/s) are computed from 10 rps aggregate, not 20,000 rps.
root_cause: Ambiguous/incorrect population basis: per-employee activity conflated with aggregate canonical workload.
correction: Rewrite as 'the 2,000-employee population produces the canonical aggregate traffic (~10 rps average, peaks ~40 rps)' or, if per-employee activity is intended, recompute all downstream rates for 20,000 rps average.
acceptance_test: Check that the stated employee count times the stated per-employee rate equals the aggregate rps used in the token-rate arithmetic.

chapter: Chapter 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference
quoted_clause: Lowering precision (FP8, or BF16 in place of FP16) does not reduce the underlying algorithmic operation count ... rather it reduces the precision, lowers the bytes transferred/stored, and can raise the effective accelerator throughput (8-bit tensor cores run at a higher peak rate).
observed: BF16 in place of FP16 does not lower bytes transferred/stored (both are 2 bytes) and does not raise H100 tensor-core peak throughput (both are 989 TFLOPS dense). The byte-reduction and higher-peak claims apply to FP8/FP4, not BF16.
evidence: FP16 = 2 bytes, BF16 = 2 bytes. H100 datasheet: FP16 and BF16 dense tensor-core peak are both 989 TFLOPS (1,979 with sparsity).
root_cause: Grouping BF16 with FP8 as a byte-reducing/higher-peak precision lever.
correction: Remove BF16 from the byte-reduction claim. Say FP8/FP4 reduce bytes and raise effective tensor-core peak; BF16 may improve numerical range but is not a bandwidth or peak-throughput lever relative to FP16 on H100.
acceptance_test: Verify that every precision named as lowering bytes or raising peak actually does so on the cited hardware.

page_hint: Chapter 2, §3 'Worked example arithmetic details', prefill levers paragraph
chapter: Chapter 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference
quoted_clause: Meeting the latency SLO therefore calls for constraint-matched levers: more GPUs (model parallelism or data parallelism)
observed: Data parallelism does not reduce a single request's prefill latency; it replicates the model and increases aggregate throughput. For a single-request TTFT SLO, only model parallelism (tensor/pipeline) or other intra-request splitting reduces the critical path.
evidence: DP runs independent replicas; a single request still executes on one replica. The chapter's own per-request feasibility framing requires reducing one request's prefill time.
root_cause: Conflating throughput scaling (DP) with latency reduction (MP).
correction: Replace 'model parallelism or data parallelism' with 'model parallelism (tensor/pipeline) for per-request latency; data parallelism increases aggregate throughput but does not reduce a single request's TTFT.'
acceptance_test: Check that every lever listed for meeting a single-request latency SLO actually shortens that request's critical path.

page_hint: Chapter 2, §3 'Worked example arithmetic details', decode bandwidth paragraph
chapter: Chapter 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference
quoted_clause: meeting that latency target calls for multi-GPU scaling or bandwidth-increasing topologies (e.g., NVLink-connected nodes)
observed: NVLink increases GPU-to-GPU interconnect bandwidth, not per-GPU HBM bandwidth. It helps tensor parallelism by making sharding/communication cheaper, but it does not increase the HBM read rate that the decode weight-streaming bottleneck depends on.
evidence: The bottleneck stated immediately above is HBM bandwidth (3.35 TB/s per GPU). NVLink is an interconnect fabric between GPUs.
root_cause: Conflating interconnect bandwidth with memory bandwidth.
correction: Say 'multi-GPU scaling (more HBM channels in aggregate) or GPUs with higher HBM bandwidth; NVLink reduces the communication cost of tensor parallelism but does not raise per-GPU HBM bandwidth.'
acceptance_test: Verify that the proposed remedy addresses the named resource (HBM bandwidth) rather than a different resource (interconnect bandwidth).

chapter: Chapter 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference
quoted_clause: KV 24.1 GB per request against the 640 GB pool
observed: 24.1 GB corresponds to ~9.2K tokens at the house FP16 KV convention (~2.62 MB/token). The canonical request is ~9.2K input + ~300 output = ~9.5K tokens, which would be ~24.9 GB. The figure appears to count input tokens only.
evidence: 2.62 MB/token × 9,200 ≈ 24.1 GB; × 9,500 ≈ 24.9 GB. The chapter elsewhere defines the request as 9.2K input + 300 output.
root_cause: KV residency computed at prefill only but labeled 'per request' without stating the token basis.
correction: Either label the number 'KV at end of prefill (9.2K tokens)' or use ~24.9 GB for full-request KV residency including the 300 generated tokens.
acceptance_test: Recompute KV from the stated token count and precision; verify the label matches the token basis used.

page_hint: Chapter 3 §1, §2, §3, §6, §8; Tables 3-2 and 3-3; boxed rule; Qwen transfer; mini-case
quoted_clause: A 70B dense model reads all 70B weights (or close to it) for every token
observed: The chapter repeatedly treats weight-read traffic as a per-token quantity: 'reads all 70B weights ... for every token'; 'FP16 active weight-read per token ~25.6 GB'; 'active weight-read traffic (~25.6 GB of weights read per token)'; '~12 GB read per token'; '~25.6 GB of active weight footprint is read per token'; Table 3-3 'FP16 weight-read per token'.
evidence: Weight traffic is per forward pass, not per token. In prefill, the same weight matrix is read once for the whole chunk of tokens; in batched decode, weights are read once per batch step, not once per sequence token. For MoE, different tokens in a batch may route to different experts, so the union of expert weights read per batch step is not simply the per-token active set. The printed per-token numbers are correct only for batch=1 single-token decode and are misleading for prefill or batched serving.
root_cause: Conflation of per-token compute (FLOPs) with per-forward-pass weight traffic. The chapter correctly distinguishes total vs active parameters but then reuses 'per token' for a bandwidth quantity that is amortized across tokens in a batch or prefill chunk.
correction: Introduce a third accounting line: 'weight-read per forward pass' or 'weight-read per batch step'. State explicitly that the 140 GB / 25.6 GB figures are batch=1 single-token decode values; for prefill or batch size B, weight traffic is amortized and, for MoE, depends on the union of routed experts. Replace 'read per token' with 'read per forward pass (batch=1 decode)' or 'per-token amortized at batch size B' wherever the claim is not scoped to batch=1.
acceptance_test: Every occurrence of 'weight-read per token' is either explicitly scoped to batch=1 single-token decode or replaced by per-forward-pass/per-batch-step language. No sentence claims a dense 70B model reads 140 GB of weights for every token in a batched or prefill forward pass.

page_hint: Chapter 3 §7, 'What We Still Don't Know', first bullet
quoted_clause: the actual fraction of active parameters may vary with prompt content, token position, and expert availability
observed: The text says the active-parameter fraction per token may vary with prompt content, token position, and expert availability.
evidence: Under fixed top-k routing with equal-sized experts, the number of active parameters per token is fixed by the architecture: k routed experts plus shared/always-on parameters. Prompt content changes which experts are selected, not how many parameters are active. Token position does not change the count. Expert availability could change effective active count only if the implementation drops tokens or uses variable-k/capacity-limited routing; that is an implementation-specific exception, not the general case.
root_cause: Confusing the identity of the selected experts with the count of active parameters. The chapter's central total-vs-active distinction depends on the count being architectural.
correction: Rewrite the bullet to say: 'Which experts are active varies with prompt content and token position; the number of active parameters per token is fixed by top-k and expert size under standard routing. Effective active count can vary only under variable-k, capacity dropping, or expert-unavailable fallback, which should be stated as an implementation-specific exception.'
acceptance_test: The text no longer claims that the active-parameter fraction varies with prompt content under fixed top-k routing; any variability claim is explicitly tied to variable-k, capacity dropping, or expert unavailability.

quoted_clause: where that shape is not known, as if the model were dense (the conservative bound)
observed: The key takeaway says that when attention shape is unknown, provision KV as if the model were dense, calling that the conservative bound.
evidence: Dense vs MoE is orthogonal to attention shape. A dense model can use GQA/MQA and have a much smaller KV cache than a dense full-MHA model. The conservative bound is full multi-head attention at the same layer count and hidden width, not merely 'dense'. The mini-case later correctly says 'dense full-MHA rate', which exposes the inconsistency.
root_cause: Using 'dense' as shorthand for 'full-MHA' in a context where the chapter has just taught that attention shape, not routing, sets KV bytes.
correction: Replace 'as if the model were dense' with 'as if the model used full multi-head attention at the same layer count and hidden width' or 'at the dense full-MHA rate'. Keep 'dense' for parameter allocation only.
acceptance_test: The key takeaway and any parallel wording distinguish parameter allocation (dense/MoE) from attention shape (full-MHA/GQA/MQA) and identify full-MHA, not dense, as the conservative KV bound.

quoted_clause: FLOPs per forward pass (approx.) | ~0.14T
observed: Tables 3-1, 3-2, and 3-3 label the FLOP figure 'per forward pass' while the derivation is 70B × 2 FLOP/param and 12.8B × 2 FLOP/param, which is per token, not per forward pass over the 9.2K-token input.
evidence: For a 9.2K-token prefill, FLOPs are approximately 9,200 × 0.14T for the dense model, not 0.14T. The table's 'per forward pass' wording is ambiguous and, read literally, wrong by a factor of the sequence length. The same ambiguity appears in the MoE table and Table 3-3.
root_cause: The table header was not updated when the arithmetic was scoped to per-token accounting.
correction: Change the metric label to 'FLOPs per token (batch=1 decode)' or 'FLOPs per token forward pass'. If a per-sequence figure is intended, multiply by the token count and label it 'FLOPs per 9.2K-token prefill'.
acceptance_test: Every FLOP table row states whether the value is per token or per sequence, and the derivation matches the label.

quoted_clause: Routing still emits one key and one value per token per layer
observed: The text attributes K/V emission to routing: 'Routing still emits one key and one value per token per layer'.
evidence: Routing selects experts in the feed-forward sub-layer. It does not emit keys or values. The attention sub-layer emits K/V. The sentence's intended point is correct—MoE routing does not change the number of K/V tensors—but the causal attribution is wrong and could confuse a reader trying to build the mental model.
root_cause: Sloppy subject assignment in a sentence whose technical point is otherwise correct.
correction: Replace with: 'The attention layers still emit one key and one value per token per layer; routing in the feed-forward sub-layer neither reduces nor increases that count.'
acceptance_test: The text no longer says routing emits K/V; K/V emission is attributed to attention layers.

page_hint: Chapter 3 §6, 'One verified 2026 transfer: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next', KV cache bullet
quoted_clause: QSA attends sparsely at micro-block granularity — so per-token KV no longer follows the dense formula
observed: The text says Qwen's hybrid attention attacks the KV constant at the mechanism level because GDN keeps a fixed-size recurrent state and QSA attends sparsely, and concludes that per-token KV no longer follows the dense formula.
evidence: Sparse attention reduces the number of key/value pairs attended during computation; it does not by itself reduce the number of K/V tensors that must be stored unless the implementation also uses a compressed, evicted, or block-sparse cache. GDN layers clearly change state growth. QSA layers may still store full K/V for all tokens. The sentence conflates sparse attention compute with KV-cache residency. If QSA does reduce cache residency, the mechanism must be stated; if it only sparsifies attention reads, the conclusion is wrong for those layers.
root_cause: Non sequitur from 'attends sparsely' to 'per-token KV no longer follows the dense formula'.
correction: Separate the two mechanisms: 'GDN layers keep a fixed-size recurrent state, so their per-token KV does not grow linearly. QSA layers sparsify attention reads; whether they also reduce stored KV depends on the cache implementation. If QSA stores full K/V, those layers still follow the dense per-token KV formula.' Cite the QSA cache mechanism or remove the claim that QSA changes the KV constant.
acceptance_test: The text states explicitly whether QSA changes KV residency or only attention compute; it does not infer reduced KV storage from sparse attention alone.

page_hint: Chapter 3 §8, mini-case, second paragraph and final paragraph
quoted_clause: we provision at the dense-model rate (~12 GB at 8-bit, ~24 GB at FP16) either way as the conservative bound
observed: The mini-case first says 'where the shape is not known we provision at the dense full-MHA rate', then later says 'we provision at the dense-model rate ... either way as the conservative bound' even after stating the challenger's known 32L/4096H GQA shape.
evidence: If the attention shape is known, the correct KV estimate is the model's own shape (0.6 GB at 8-bit for the challenger), not the dense full-MHA rate. 'Either way' is ambiguous: it could mean 'whether dense or MoE' (correct) or 'whether shape known or unknown' (incorrect). The surrounding text supports the former, but the wording invites the latter.
root_cause: Compression of two different conditions—dense-vs-MoE and shape-known-vs-unknown—into one phrase.
correction: Rewrite: 'When the attention shape is unknown, provision at the dense full-MHA rate as the conservative bound. When the shape is known—as it is for the challenger—use the model's own shape. Routing does not change the bytes either way.'
acceptance_test: The mini-case no longer says to use the dense rate when the shape is known; the condition for the conservative bound is explicitly 'shape unknown'.

quoted_clause: Controlled comparison: same context length and cache dtype — while weight residency ... and the attention shape ... all differ
observed: The caption calls the comparison 'controlled' while listing three variables that differ: weight residency, active-compute fraction, and attention shape.
evidence: A controlled comparison holds all but one variable fixed. Here the KV difference is correctly attributed to attention shape, but the comparison is not controlled for shape; it is a side-by-side contrast with confounded variables. The caption then explains the confound, so the technical point survives, but the word 'controlled' is misleading.
root_cause: Using 'controlled' to mean 'same context length and cache dtype' rather than 'all relevant variables held fixed'.
correction: Replace 'Controlled comparison' with 'Side-by-side contrast holding context length and cache dtype fixed' or 'Comparison with context length and cache dtype held fixed'.
acceptance_test: The caption no longer calls the comparison controlled while listing multiple differing variables.

quoted_clause: in MoE pre-training, a routing loss directs each token to the most relevant expert(s), and the unused experts receive no gradient for that step
observed: The text describes MoE training as a 'routing loss' that directs each token to the most relevant experts and says unused experts receive no gradient for that step.
evidence: MoE routers are trained end-to-end through a gating network; there is typically an auxiliary load-balancing loss, not a routing loss that directly assigns tokens. Unused experts receive no gradient from that token, but the phrasing 'routing loss directs each token' suggests a supervised assignment mechanism that is not how standard MoE training works. The simplification is not central to deployment, but it is technically imprecise in a chapter that otherwise demands exactness.
root_cause: Compressed training description that conflates learned gating with a direct routing objective.
correction: Rewrite: 'In MoE pre-training, a learned gating network selects top-k experts per token; an auxiliary load-balancing loss is usually added to encourage expert use. Experts not selected for a given token receive no gradient from that token at that step.'
acceptance_test: The text no longer describes a 'routing loss' that directly directs tokens; it distinguishes learned gating from auxiliary load balancing.

quoted_clause: ~21× less than Qwen's own total weight footprint (~250 GB → 12 GB)
observed: The text says Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 125B total plus a separate 51B of offloadable N-gram embedding parameters, then compares active weight traffic to 'Qwen's own total weight footprint (~250 GB)'.
evidence: 250 GB is 125B × 2 bytes. If the 51B N-gram parameters are part of the model's total weight footprint when not offloaded, the full footprint is ~352 GB, not ~250 GB. The text later says 'plus the offloadable N-gram', so the 250 GB figure is the core MoE footprint, not the full total. The ratio is therefore against a scoped subset, not the full model.
root_cause: Inconsistent scope for 'total weight footprint' after introducing a separate offloadable parameter block.
correction: Label the 250 GB figure as 'core 125B MoE weight footprint' and state that the 51B N-gram block adds ~102 GB if resident. If the 21× ratio is meant against the core only, say so explicitly.
acceptance_test: The text distinguishes core MoE weights from the offloadable N-gram block and does not call the 250 GB figure the full total weight footprint without qualification.

chapter: Chapter 4 — The Anatomy of an AI Workload
quoted_clause: A workload is defined by six orthogonal dimensions ... Together they form a complete specification that — taken alone — determines model selection, system architecture, and economic feasibility.
observed: The six dimensions are not orthogonal: economic constraints are largely derived from traffic, token profile, latency, and operational constraints; quality and latency interact; operational constraints affect economics. Nor do the six dimensions uniquely determine model selection or architecture; multiple architectures can satisfy the same six-dimensional characterization.
evidence: The chapter itself later shows economic constraints are computed from traffic and token profile (e.g. tokens-per-dollar, cost per request), and operational constraints (multi-region, privacy) change the economic floor. This contradicts the claim that the dimensions are orthogonal and jointly sufficient to determine architecture.
root_cause: Overclaiming the framework's mathematical status: treating a useful characterization lens as an orthogonal basis and a complete decision function.
correction: Replace 'six orthogonal dimensions' with 'six dimensions (not strictly orthogonal)' and replace 'complete specification that — taken alone — determines model selection, system architecture, and economic feasibility' with 'joint characterization that constrains model selection, system architecture, and economic feasibility; it does not uniquely determine them.'
acceptance_test: The revised paragraph no longer asserts orthogonality or unique determination; it states that the dimensions interact and that architecture decisions require additional engineering judgment and measurement.
